Issued at 1232 PM CDT Tue Sep 15 2026

THIS AFTERNOON:  Sunny skies continue Tuesday afternoon as dry air 
filters into the region.  Temperatures will continue to rise into 
the upper 60s to lower 70s. 

TONIGHT: Most notable change tonight was to continually lower dew 
points from the NBM guidance.  Short term models have done a better 
job capturing lower dew points though the region and keep surface 
winds easterly through the overnight hours.  These winds will keep 
reinforcing the middle to upper 40 dew points currently in the area. 
Mid-lvl clouds will gradually filter back into the region after 
midnight, and may lead to some stabilization of the diurnal 
temperature fall overnight. 

WEDNESDAY: A generally quiet day is on tap for the region 
Wednesday. By mid-morning the 850mb ridge axis will slide east 
of the Tri- State area allowing gradual moisture advection 
northward by mid-day. Soundings indicate a thickening low-lvl 
moisture profile through the afternoon as weak warm advection 
passes across the Tri-State area. This may result in widely 
scattered very light showers through the afternoon and evening. 
At times by the evening, a bit of patchy drizzle could also be 
possible as ceilings remain quite low and there remains weak 
warm advection at the top of the saturated layer. 

THURSDAY-FRIDAY: The most impactful weather in the next 7 days will 
take place Thursday night into Friday. Low-lvl moisture and weak 
boundary layer flow may keep clouds around the area early Thursday 
morning.  High pressure over northern Minnesota may limit the rise 
in dew points early in the morning, again which may be a deviation 
from the NBM or at least pointed towards the 25th percentile. If we 
have quite a bit of cloud cover, then the persistent easterly winds 
may prevent temperatures from reaching the middle 70s. 

Models are in strong agreement that a progressive open wave exits 
the Central Rockies and crosses the Dakotas Thursday night and 
Friday.  This system will be very much like a late Fall to early 
Winter system, bringing strong layered frontogenesis and elevated 
instability into the Tri-state area after midnight.   Deterministic 
models remain a bit variable with the northward extent of the 700mb 
forcing, with the GFS notably further north than other solutions. 
Ensemble based solutions are clustered fairly well with a corridor 
of heavy rain near Highway 14, but AI based ensembles of the GEFS/EC 
which seemed to pick up early location shifts last winter, are 
supporting of a track somewhere between Highway 14 and along 
I-90. Rainfall will be slow to leave the area on Friday, with 
some gusty northerly winds by the afternoon. Areas near the 
Missouri River and Highway 20 areas have the highest chance of 
seeing some sun in the afternoon though the current temperature 
forecast remains highly variable given track of rain. 

Given the influx of moisture northward, rainfall forecast amounts 
could rise sharply over the 24 hr period ending mid-day Friday. 
Ensembles support a greater than 40% chance of more than 2" of QPF, 
with 95 percentile data already as high as 2.50-3" wherever 
this band of precipitation falls. As we begin to ingest more 
higher resolution data sets, we'll likely see these broad areas
of high probabilities focus better, but also see those higher 
end values rise. With that said, the WPC "slight" risk of 
excessive rainfall seems warranted, with AI based outlooks 
suggesting higher risks may be possible if the forcing zone can 
be determined. This rainfall, especially as you begin to pass 
the 2-3" mark, could lead to some increases in local river 
levels, as rainfall this month has been above normal and we're 
beginning to see better responses in levels after rain ends. 

SATURDAY-MONDAY: The weekend will remain slightly unsettled as upper 
troughing lingers over the Northern Rockies. Brief shortwave 
ridging should allow most areas to dry out on Saturday, but 
feature cooler than normal temperatures. An upper low then 
drifts slowly southeast across the Dakotas into Sunday and 
Monday. Initial indications suggest the greatest lift stays over
the western Dakotas on Sunday with rain chances returning again
by Monday.
